open.question: The officer's pen broke the crew's rule of choosing in front of the ring and the law charged nothing for it: will Hesper let the officer keep the power to write a name into the book, or will it make a rule the green journal can carry on its own?

Is the name written into the green journal on the nineteenth day the name Verrin said at the roots, and is there any hand left on Hesper that can check the farm's only written name before the next flowering reads it off the page?

The keeping was made at the wall on the twenty-second day and stands in no line of the green journal, and its first year had nothing to say: will Hesper say its own dead out loud once a year, and who will be holding the names when the next flowering reads its sign?

The woman from the second shift has asked the ring to say her daughter's name once a year at the keeping — the one name the fundamental law forbids the farm to mention again: what does Hesper do with a request its own law has already answered?

closed.question: Why has the plant been asking for blood for three days and never stopped shaking?
closed.resolution: The sign for blood and the sign for iron in the water are the same stroke with one ending, and the adults wrote the old Reader's chart into the green journal; the plant was asking for clean water while the root feed line carried rust through an eaten valve seat.

closed.question: Will the farm keep the rule that the officer writes the reader's own words into the green journal, or will an officer restore the old wording?
closed.resolution: Rusk restored an adult wording for one day, wrote it with his own name under it, the plant never answered the line and stopped shaking for light instead, and the officer paid the count with a tooth and kept the reader's rule.

closed.question: What will the crew make of the officer's tooth: proof that an adult wording costs a body, or proof that the farm is being punished for the new rule?
closed.resolution: Chapter 3 settled it for the crew: the plant was never offended and never punishing, because an open green journal held up at the wall moves no leaf while a hand lamp turns the whole crown, and the price comes out of whoever wrote the line that did not come true, in the order tooth, finger, eye — Rusk paid the first price for his second line and the second price for his third.

closed.question: What name will the crew give the plant at this flowering, now that no child has died on Hesper in nine years and the only name available is the one the farm is forbidden to say again?
closed.resolution: Chapter 4 answered it as a refusal and a reform: the farm will not answer the sign with any dead child's name, because the Reader read the sign whole for the first time, called her own earlier reading a half reading, and showed that the farm had been answering its own memory of the last flowering; no line about a name goes into the green journal until the whole sign has been read in the light.

closed.question: The count has restarted on the name request and the next price is an eye: will the farm say the forbidden name, let the officer pay again, or stop writing in the green journal?
closed.resolution: Chapter 5 answered it with a fourth way and no price: the officer wrote an adult wording under the sign — the long stroke, blood over the roots until the plant is still — the crew cut four hands over the soil the same morning, the plant turned its whole crown and its open flower down to the wet ground, and on the third morning nothing was taken, because the line promised blood until the plant is still and the plant had been still for four days, so the count had no unmet request left to charge. The name was never said, the book stayed open, and the child's whole reading lost to the officer's wording in front of the crew.

closed.question: What is asked by the end of the name sign where this year's shape carries three hooks, given that the sign of the last flowering carried none at all?
closed.resolution: Chapter 6 read the end of the sign in front of the crew and against the two signs the old Reader had drawn: the hooks are the tip of the blood sign turned back toward its own stem, repeated — the mark of a thing that returns — and not a number, because the plant counts nothing and keeps no calendar; eighteen years ago the sign ended in one hook and nine years ago in none, and the farm gave both names inside a day, so the three days are the farm's own law read into somebody else's drawing.

closed.question: What is the plant asking for now that it has turned its open flower away from the crown lamps and holds it down to the soil where the blood went in, while the sign over the shelf stays unchanged?
closed.resolution: Chapter 7 answered it by measurement instead of reading: the flower was not attending to the blood, the page or the name but to the plant's own water, and its face was aimed at the seat where the root line comes up into the soil. The officer held the open book over that exact seat and moved no leaf; the boy from the water crew turned the bypass wheel there a quarter turn, and the low leaves, the crown and the open flower turned together, the flower lifted off the trench for the first time in six days, and the work ring's air gauge moved a tenth higher, its first movement since the flowering began.

closed.question: The officer's sixth line stands under the name sign with the count restarted on it and nothing left on the ladder above an eye: what does the law take from the officer, from the farm, or from nobody when the third day comes again?
closed.resolution: Chapter 8 answered it with a pen and not with a body: on the nineteenth day the officer wrote a seventh line over the same sign, and a new line under a sign takes the charge off the line above it while leaving that line standing, so the third morning of the twenty-first brought no price, the officer kept the rest of his face, and Hesper still does not know what its ladder holds above an eye because nothing was ever charged a fourth time. The farm learned the way off the ladder instead of the top of it.

closed.question: If the name given at this flowering exists only in Verrin's memory, what happens on Hesper when she is dead and the next flowering asks for a name that no living hand holds?
closed.resolution: Chapter 8 took the farm off that memory: the officer entered the name in the green journal from his own hearing of the one saying at the roots, so the next flowering will read a page and not a head. What the farm bought is a name that no living hand can confirm — Verrin refused to read the entry or to say the name a second time to check his ear — so the silence she was paid for is now a written name standing in the book beside a register that keeps only holes.

closed.question: What does the plant need from its own root line at the seat, given that a quarter turn of the wheel lifted its flower off the trench and moved the farm's gauge for the first time in nine days, and what does the farm owe it now that it has a measurement instead of a reading?
closed.resolution: Chapter 9 answered it with water and a number: the plant wanted nothing from the farm that a page or a reading could give, the child said out loud in front of the crew that the small shape at the root line is turned at the water and not at the ring, and the farm put two hands on the root line before every shift with the reading written into the doctor's column — what Hesper owes the plant is clean water at the seat, and its instrument is a wheel and a gauge and not a book.

closed.question: What does the small new shape at the root line ask, come up in the leaves along the water while the rest of the wall lies flat, and what does a farm that has never seen its plant stop asking do with a plant that has nothing to demand?
closed.resolution: Chapter 9 answered it as a refusal to be a request: the Reader read the small shape in front of the ring as turned at the water and not at the farm, the flower lay closed on the same seat, and the farm had nothing to answer for the first morning in the book — the shape asks the ring for nothing, and the plant asking again is left to the plant's own body.

promises.promise: Doctor Meren promised Bea that nobody will open a hand again on a reading she has not spoken at the roots, in front of witnesses, in her own voice.
promises.resolution: Chapter 2: the boy from the water crew offered his hand on the second morning of the flowering and Meren refused it in front of the whole crew, because the Reader had not spoken; no hand was opened, and the officer paid the count himself.

promises.promise: Iven promised Bea that he will draw her the signs he read in the years he was the Reader, on the crate in the low ring, and that she is to come without the doctor and without the green journal, so that she learns what he read and not what the farm wrote down.
promises.resolution: Chapter 6: the child came down to the stores without the doctor and without the book, and Iven drew both signs he had read — the flowering of eighteen years ago, which ended in a single hook, and the one of nine years ago, which ended in nothing — and then carried the crate up to the root wall himself so that the ring could read them.

promises.promise: Verrin's term, accepted by the crew in front of the ring: when the Reader is old enough to hold it, she is to be told that a name of a dead child was spent at the roots and that she will never be given it, so that the farm's silence is a thing it knows and not a hole in it. Since chapter 8 the name also stands written in the green journal she walks past every morning, so the silence now rests on the fact that she cannot read written words.
promises.resolution: Chapter 9: at the end of the twenty-second day Verrin paid the last term of her own bargain in the trench — a name was spent at the roots on the fifteenth day, it stands in no page the child can read, and it will never be given to her — and the child answered by asking for the farm's dead to be said to her from now on, so the silence is now a thing she knows and the keeping has its first mouth.

deferred_answers.question: Which dead child gave the plant the name it carries now, and what was done to the crew's memory of her?
deferred_answers.reason: Answered in the flowering episode itself, as the reason for deferring said it would be.
deferred_answers.resolution: Chapter 4: the child was the daughter of the woman from the second shift, seven years old when she died; her name was taken off the register page in the low ring, off her slate and off every wall of the farm by Iven himself in the year of the chart, and no one on Hesper has said it since.

deferred_answers.question: What line did Iven write in the green journal nine years ago, and what sign did he read at that flowering, that he will not explain to the child?
deferred_answers.reason: The answer spends the last flowering, which is the ground the farm is standing on in chapters 5 and 6; he himself has promised to draw it for her without the doctor and without the book.
deferred_answers.resolution: Chapter 6: he read the flowering sign with the long stroke and nothing at its end, wrote his reading in the green journal, and under it a line promising that the farm would keep the named child among its own; the farm gave the child to the flower and then took her off the register page, the slate and the walls, which is the opposite of keeping, so the line failed within three days and the book took his tooth — a line is a debt of its writer whether it asks for something or promises something.

deferred_answers.question: Whether a line the farm can always keep ends a request in the law's own terms or only on the page, and what the count does when a request is answered with a wording and the plant's body never agrees with it.
deferred_answers.reason: The farm now owns a page that can always be paid and the plant's own sign has not changed by a stroke; answering this in chapter 5 would replace the test the reader has to watch with a statement, so the test is handed to the air gauge and to the crew's next reading.
deferred_answers.resolution: Chapter 7 answered it in two parts. On the page the line held: nobody charged a price for the fourth line of chapter 5 and nobody charged one for the naming entry of chapter 6, so a wording the farm can always keep closes the count in the law's own terms. Off the page it answered nothing: through the whole week in which the farm wrote, bled and named, the plant moved no leaf for a page, not even when the officer held the open book over the exact place its open flower was aimed. The request stays on the wall where the count stopped, and the farm found out only when the doctor's gauge moved — a tenth, on the day a hand turned the wheel at the root line.

deferred_answers.question: Whether a name said once at the roots can be kept out of the farm's speech for the rest of Verrin's life, and what the law does if the name is said again by her or by anyone else who heard it.
deferred_answers.reason: The farm has just bought this silence with a whole year of its register and has never tested what the silence costs the one who keeps it; answering it in chapter 6 would turn the naming into a rule instead of a price, and the price is what the reader has to watch at the roots.
deferred_answers.resolution: Chapter 8 answered it with a pen: the name went into the green journal in the officer's own hand, written on the morning he refused to let it be said out loud, and the law charged nobody anything for it — the count runs on lines that are not kept and on nothing else, so Hesper's whole silence around a name is the farm's rule and has never had a price of its own. The silence now rests on the fact that no one says the written name, not on anything the plant or the law does about it.

deferred_answers.question: What the law takes when the ladder of prices has run out: the officer's sixth line stands unmet with an eye already paid for it, and no one on Hesper has ever seen a fourth charge.
deferred_answers.reason: The farm has just discovered that the ladder ends, and what happens above an eye is the price of the whole rule of writing; saying it now would replace the three days the reader has to watch with a statement. Chapter 8 closed the count before the fourth charge could ever be made, so the answer is still unpaid and the farm still has no record above an eye.

deferred_answers.question: What the law does with a line that comes true after its count has run out: the promise Iven wrote nine years ago was that the farm would keep the child it was naming, and the keeping made on the twenty-second day is the first thing on Hesper that could still keep it.
deferred_answers.reason: Chapter 10 emptied the book of names and refused the one name that promise was about, and the child carried both facts to the ring; the answer spends the keeping and the future of that refusal, and saying it now would turn the farm's newest rule into a verdict on a line nobody has read since.

deferred_answers.question: Whether the flower hears a spoken name at all, given that the farm has never tested it and that its whole silence around the name it gave is a rule with no price on it.
deferred_answers.reason: The answer undoes the ground the farm's ritual of silence stands on, and the reader has to watch the ring try to put a name into its own keeping before it can be told that the plant has no ear for words at all; the mother's request, which is due sooner, stands first.
